paper_title: WAM-Policy: World Action Models with On-Policy Distillation for Quadrupedal Loco-Manipulation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Arm-free quadrupeds can perform loco-manipulation, walking on three legs while manipulating with a front leg, yet no existing policy for it follows language instructions. World action models (WAMs) have emerged as effective language-conditioned manipulation policies, but are pretrained for robot arms and sample slowly. WAM-Policy turns one WAM into a quadrupedal loco-manipulation policy via two stages. The first, Cross-Morphology Policy Adaptation and Acceleration, adapts the arm-centric WAM to quadrupeds and distills the transferred policy into a student with one video and two action steps by on-policy self-distillation (OPSD). This student, however, is bounded by its teacher, which only imitates demonstrations. The second stage, Task-Specific Improvement and Merging, therefore tunes the teacher by reinforcement learning (RL) and merges the slow specialists into one few-step student by multi-teacher on-policy distillation (M-OPD). On QLM-Bench, ten simulated tasks with 1,000 demonstrations synthesized without teleoperation, the transferred policy reaches 77.0%, and the OPSD student keeps 76.7% while sampling 14 times faster. Task-specific RL and M-OPD lift it to 85.0%. We also deploy the OPSD student on a real Unitree Go2 Air. WAM-Policy thus achieves a stronger quadrupedal policy at a fraction of the inference cost.

sections.content: 1. Introduction Arm-free quadrupeds can perform loco-manipulation, walking on three legs while manipulating with front leg, yet no existing policy for it follows language instructions. World action models (WAMs) have emerged as effective language-conditioned manipulation policies, but are pretrained for robot arms and sample slowly. WAM-Policy turns one WAM into quadrupedal loco-manipulation policy via two stages. The first, Cross-Morphology Policy Adaptation and Acceleration, adapts the arm-centric WAM to quadrupeds and distills the transferred policy into student with one video and two action steps by onpolicy self-distillation (OPSD). This student, however, is bounded by its teacher, which only imitates demonstrations. The second stage, Task-Specific Improvement and Merging, therefore tunes the teacher by reinforcement learning (RL) and merges the slow specialists into one few-step student by multi-teacher on-policy distillation (M-OPD). On QLM-Bench, ten simulated tasks with 1,000 demonstrations synthesized without teleoperation, the transferred policy reaches 77.0%, and the OPSD student keeps 76.7% while sampling 14 times faster. Task-specific RL and M-OPD lift it to 85.0%. We also deploy the OPSD student on real Unitree Go2 Air. WAM-Policy thus achieves stronger quadrupedal policy at fraction of the inference cost. Code & Website. Quadrupeds reach terrain that wheeled and fixed-base robots cannot, and language is natural way to instruct them. To manipulate, most quadrupeds carry an arm or gripper [15, 32, 59], but an arm-free quadruped can also walk on three legs and use front leg as the endeffector [3, 9, 10]. Manipulating with leg spares the robot the weight and mechanical complexity of an added arm [3]. Existing visual planners for such leg manipulation learn from point clouds and cannot map language instructions to actions end to end [16, 17], and, to our knowledge, no demonstrations with language instructions exist for this setting. Meanwhile, world action models (WAMs), which jointly predict future observations and actions, have emerged as effective language-conditioned manipulation policies [6, 14, 21, 24, 57, 61, 74]. This paper brings WAM to arm-free quadrupedal loco-manipulation  (Fig. 1)  . This raises two challenges. First, pretrained WAMs are arm-centric, and their multi-step sampling is slow. Our base WAM, LingBot-VA [24], sees head and wrist cameras and emits 30-dimensional dual-arm command, whereas the cameras of quadruped move with its body and its manipulating leg also supports it. Its video and action streams are each sampled over many steps at one network function evaluation (NFE) per step, so our transferred policy needs 2.226 for chunk that covers 0.32 of robot time, and sampling with one video and two action steps lowers its success. On the real robot, the body drifts while the whole-body controller [9] balances it during sampling, so actions computed from the state before sampling no longer fit the state after it. Second, the distilled policy remains bounded by imitation. distilled student is bounded by its teacher, which only imitates demonstrations and still fails on some hard tasks. Reinforcement learning with task-specific rewards can go beyond the demonstrations, but it tunes the slow high-NFE policy one task at time, so it yields several slow specialists that must be merged into one policy and accelerated again. WAM-Policy turns one WAM into quadrupedal locomanipulation policy via two stages, one for each challenge: Cross-Morphology Policy Adaptation and Acceleration (Stage 1) and Task-Specific Improvement and Merging (Stage 2). Both stages end by distilling high-NFE teacher, the policy itself in Stage 1 and the task-routed teachers in Stage 2, on-policy into 1/2-NFE student (one video and two action steps), so the final policy is stronger than the transferred one at fraction of its inference cost. Our contributions are: Cross-morphology adaptation and acceleration. Stage 1 replaces only the visual and action interfaces of WAM, fine-tunes it on quadruped demonstrations, and accelerates it by few-step form of on-policy selfdistillation (OPSD) [69], in which the same network with more sampling steps labels the students own samples. The transferred policy reaches 77.0%, and the OPSD student keeps 76.7% (69.3% without distillation) while sampling 14 times faster. Task-specific improvement and merging. Stage 2 tunes specialist teachers by per-task reinforcement learning and merges them by multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) [40], which routes each context to the teacher of its task. On pushing box and opening door, the specialists succeed in every episode, against 47% and 53% for the OPSD teacher, and the M-OPD student reaches 90% and 87%, raising the ten-task success from 76.7% to 85.0%, above the OPSD teacher (77.0%). QLM-Bench, ten simulated loco-manipulation tasks with 1,000 language-annotated demonstrations synthesized without teleoperation, and evaluation in simulation and on real Unitree Go2 Air, where the OPSD student runs without real-robot data. 2. Related Work Quadrupedal loco-manipulation. Quadrupeds that follow language mostly pair VLA/VLM with controller for velocity, gait, or navigation [8, 11, 53, 68], while manipulation systems attach an arm or gripper [15, 32, 39, 59], sequence skills via an LLM [43], or track foot targets with leg controllers [3, 9, 10]. Visual leg-manipulation planners learn from point clouds by reinforcement learning [16] or imitation (Leg-Manip [17]) without language; WAM-Policy is single language-conditioned RGB policy. World action models. World action models (WAMs) jointly predict future scenes and actions using videopretrained priors [6, 14, 21, 57, 61, 74], including our base model LingBot-VA [24]. Prior WAMs target fixedbase arms, humanoids [26, 27, 45, 65, 70], or an armed wheeled-legged quadruped [37], and quadruped world models address locomotion or navigation [4, 22, 58]; none manipulates with load-bearing leg. Rather than training cross-embodiment policy [12, 42, 54], we adapt one armcentric WAMto our knowledge the first WAM for armfree quadrupedal loco-manipulation. Few-step WAMs and on-policy distillation. Multi-step joint denoising makes WAMs strong but slow [21, 24, 61]; unlike methods that skip full future prediction [25, 36, 38, 51, 64, 66, 70], we accelerate the latent plan so that the teacher can supervise it. Few-step distillation [34, 35, 44, 48, 50, 56, 62, 63] has been applied offline to WAMs by Flash-WAM [2] and concurrent DirectWAM [72] and AnyStep-WAM [55], whereas on-policy training supervises student on its own samples [1, 5, 20, 47]. Existing onpolicy WAM/VLA distillation either labels single rollout batch [60], preserves the step count [33, 40], or runs onpolicy only along the denoising chain [41]. Whereas prior on-policy self-distillation grants the teacher privileged context [30, 69], our OPSD teacher uses the same closed-loop context with more sampling steps, distilling the student to one video and two action steps along its own denoising chain. learning and policy merging. ReinReinforcement forcement learning fine-tunes diffusion and flow models [31, 71] and policies [46, 67], including VLAs [7, 23], and lets policy go beyond its demonstrations; it is best used to adjust an already competent policy [19]. Tuning one task at time, however, yields several specialists; MultiTeacher OPD [40] distills several teachers into one student but keeps their step count, whereas M-OPD merges the specialists into one few-step student. 3. Setup QLM-Bench (Quadrupedal Loco-Manipulation Benchmark) is MuJoCo benchmark for language-conditioned loco-manipulation in which Unitree Go2 manipulates with its front-left leg, with the two cameras, the commands, and the whole-body controller of Sec. 3.1.1. The benchmark has ten tasks  (Fig. 4)  : close fridge door, close an oven door, turn valve, pull open drawer, open room door, press button, lift basket, kick ball through goal, push box into target area, and sweep block into target area. Evaluation protocol. We evaluate on QLM-Bench (Sec. 4) with its Standard100 protocol: ten held-out scene configurations (cases) per task, time limit of 24 to 60 per task, and policy seeds 42, 43, and 44 on each case, for 300 episodes per policy. policy seed only sets the initial noise of the policy, while the case fixes the scene, its reset, and the physics. Simulation waits for the policy at every chunk, so success rates do not depend on inference speed. Paired McNemar tests between the policies are in Sec. I. Demonstration synthesis. For each task, large multimodal model drafts reference trajectory of commands from short description of the task (Fig. 2, bottom left). After human review, the reference is retargeted to randomized scenes and executed by C, and the successful episodes are kept as demonstrations, with neither teleoperation nor handdesigned trajectories. This gives 1,000 demonstrations, 100 per task, each recording the two camera streams, the executed commands, and language instruction. We will release the benchmark and the demonstrations with our code. 5. Experiments The experiments test that Stage 1 yields competent quadruped policy (Sec. 5.2.1) that samples faster than real time without losing this competence (Sec. 5.2.2). They then test that Stage 2.1 yields specialist teachers that outperform the OPSD teacher on their own tasks, that Stage 2.2 merges them into one 1/2-NFE student that keeps most of their gains (Sec. 5.3), and that the OPSD student runs on real robot (Sec. 5.5). sections.content: The OPSD student matches but does not exceed its teacher, so Stage 2.1 tunes the transferred policy on two tasks on which it often fails, pushing the box (47%) and opening the door (53%). Each specialist teacher succeeds in all 30 episodes of its own task (Tab. 1); its training curves are in Fig. S1. Stage 2.2 merges both by M-OPD into one 1/2NFE student, which learns the other eight tasks from the OPSD teacher (Sec. 3.2.2). The M-OPD student pushes the box in 90% and opens the door in 87% of the episodes, against 50% and 37% for the OPSD student, so it keeps most of the gain of its specialist teachers; on each of the other eight tasks it differs from the OPSD student by at most one episode, and it still never sweeps the block, which 5.4. Ablation Training contexts. We vary the source of the training contexts through η (Tab. 2): the teacher cache alone already supervises the student on its own samples, and streaming contexts add those that it reaches in closed loop (Sec. 3.1.2). All three students recover the teacher at 1/2 NFE, with 76.3% to 77.0% against 77.0%, so OPSD is not sensitive to the source of its contexts: the recovery comes from the objective that the three share, the same-noise regression along the students own sampling chain. We use the equal mixture by default. Number of updates. We train beyond the default 300 updates to test whether the student keeps improving (Tab. 3). With the teacher cache only, 2,000 updates give 77 successes in 100 episodes against 79 after 300, and with the default mixture, 900 updates give 79 against 82. The distillation loss on held-out contexts keeps falling slowly over these updates (Fig. S2), but the closed-loop success does not follow it, so we keep the default 300 updates. In this configuration, matching distributions thus does not recover the success that the same-noise regression does. Sampling steps. We reduce the sampling steps of the teachers parameters without any distillation, to locate where the loss of success begins (Tab. 5). With 2/4 NFE the success is 78.0%, as high as the 77.0% with 25/50 NFE, and only the last halving to 1/2 NFE lowers it, to 69.3%. OPSD recovers this last halving: its student reaches 76.7% with half the network evaluations of 2/4 NFE, and the same distillation is what merges the specialists in Stage 2. Proprioception. Both cameras are mounted on the body, so their views shake as the robot moves, and we test whether proprioceptive state reduces the noise that this shaking adds to the video stream. We add 10-dimensional proprioceptive state to the inputs and predictions of the teacher, trained otherwise identically (Tab. 6, Sec. C). It succeeds in 67 of 100 episodes against 77: it pushes the box in all 10 episodes but neither turns the valve nor opens the door, which the RGB-only teacher does in all 10. Predicting the state jointly with the video and the action thus lowers success, so WAM-Policy observes RGB only. 5.5. Real-Robot Deployment We deploy the OPSD student on Unitree Go2 Air with the two cameras of Sec. 3.1.1: the ego view comes from the Go2s built-in camera and the top-down view from RealSense D435i. The command interface and the wholebody controller are those of the simulation, and the student runs off-board, with the VAE, on workstation with single RTX 5070 Ti that connects to the robot by wired Ethernet. The policy is trained only on simulated data from QLM-Bench and sees no real-robot data. We test three tasks with ten trials each, and the OPSD student succeeds in 7 of 30 trials overall (Tab. 7). Figure 5 compares key frames of real-robot and simulated rollouts of these tasks, and Fig. 1 (top) shows time-lapse composites of real-robot rollouts. On this workstation, sampling takes 0.159 per chunk, but the closed loop takes 0.66 with the encoding of the observations; since this exceeds the 0.32 of chunk, the robot holds its last command between chunks. 6. Conclusion We presented WAM-Policy, which turns an arm-centric world action model into language-conditioned policy for quadrupedal loco-manipulation. Stage 1 adapts the WAM to quadrupeds and distills it into few-step student by OPSD, which is bounded by its teacher. Stage 2 therefore tunes the transferred policy into specialist teachers by reinforcement learning and merges them by M-OPD into one 1/2-NFE student that is stronger than the transferred policy (85.0% against 77.0%) at fraction of its inference cost. We further build QLM-Bench, ten quadrupedal loco-manipulation tasks with demonstrations synthesized without teleoperation, and evaluate WAM-Policy in simulation and on real quadruped.

Implementation Details This section completes the implementation details of Sec. 5.1 for QLM-Bench. Fine-tuning. We fine-tune for 5,000 updates on 80 demonstrations per task and hold out the other 20. The re-initialized input embedding and output projection of the action stream take the 9-dimensional command in place of the 30-dimensional dual-arm vector of LingBot-VA, which consists of end-effector poses, joint angles, and gripper commands. Figure S4 shows the losses of this fine-tuning: the validation loss falls from 0.209 to 0.053 for the video stream and from 1.37 to 0.0012 for the action stream, and most of each decrease, 72% and 83% of the drop in log loss, occurs within the first 1,000 updates. Distillation. has rank 256, and the teacher cache holds about 5,000 contexts. OPSD draws 24 streaming and 24 cached contexts per update (η = 0.5 in Eq. (3)). M-OPD starts from the EMA weights of the OPSD student after 300 updates and trains for another 300 updates with the settings of OPSD; the optimizer state, the warm-up, and the EMA start anew. As in OPSD, streaming environments are balanced over tasks; specialist contexts replace the cache entries of their tasks one for one. Neither the teacher nor the student uses classifier-free guidance, and every student is evaluated with EMA weights after 300 updates unless stated otherwise. Hyperparameters. All steps use AdamW with linear warm-up to constant learning rate. Stage 1.1 fine-tunes the transformer with learning rate of 1 105. OPSD and M-OPD train the LoRA update with learning rate of 3 105, with = 103 and λA = 1 in Eq. (2), and keep an EMA of the trained weights with decay 0.99. Each specialist of Stage 2.1 trains LoRA update of rank 32 with learning rate of 1 104, for 15 rounds of 24 updates. Each camera renders 640 360 RGB at 50 Hz; the model takes every fourth frame, resized to 320 180 per view, and the two views are stacked vertically after the VAE. chunk holds one latent, which covers four such frames, and 16 commands at 50 Hz. command consists of the planar base velocity (m/s) and yaw rate (rad/s), the target position of the front-left foot (m), and its target force (N); the velocity and position dimensions are normalized with their 1st and 99th percentiles over the training demonstrations. All samplers use Euler steps on uniform grid of noise levels with flow shift of 5 for the video stream and 1 for the action stream, and attend to window of 8 past video and action units. Leg-Manip. The per-task planners of Leg-Manip use 4 to 80 successful demonstrations per task, only 4 for pushing the box and 5 for sweeping the block; opening the door has none. Over the nine tasks with demonstrations, its mean success is 68.6%. Specialist teachers. Each specialist of Tab. 1 is applied on all ten tasks. The push-box specialist is the update after the last round of Stage 2.1, chosen without looking at the evaluation; the open-door specialist is the update after round 4, chosen on 32 held-out episodes of training, not on Standard100. Outside its tuned task, the push-box specialist pulls the drawer open in 21 of 30 episodes against 29 for the OPSD teacher, and the open-door specialist sweeps the block in 16 of 30 against none. Both differences remain when the OPSD teacher is evaluated again on the second workstation with batched inference (Sec. G): it pulls the drawer open in 29 of 30 episodes and never sweeps the block. G. Compute Resources Training time. Each training run uses one node with eight GPUs. The fine-tuning of Stage 1.1 takes about 14 hours, OPSD about 8 hours for the 300 updates of the student in Tab. 1, the two specialist teachers of Stage 2.1 about 5 and 9 hours, and M-OPD about 5 hours, shorter than OPSD because the collection of its streaming contexts was optimized.
